translations.text: The life of our beloved brother Apa Paul of Tamma, who entered into rest on the seventh day of the month of Paope. May his blessing come upon us, and may we be saved in the peace of God. Amen. Listen, you who love to listen, to the voice [?].
[?] worthy [?], just as he said to his disciples, “If you keep my commandments [?], you will remain in them [?].”
God sent Michael the archangel to me at noon on the sixteenth of Epip. He said to me, “Greetings, my honored son.” I answered him, “Greetings [?].”
[?] is the man of Tamma, for you are the one who will take charge of his body when he lays his body down.
When he had said these things, he went to heaven in glory. I immediately got up and stopped [?].
[?] is equal [?]. John said, “Let it be so, our father and our bishop.” Peter said, “My father Paul, get up and call upon God to send us bread
from heaven, so that we may eat together.” My father said, “Forgive me. Bless me. Get up, and let us pray to him, and he will grant our request.” They got up and stretched out their hands
together. My father called upon God, saying, “My Lord Jesus Christ, you who blessed five loaves, and five hundred people ate and went away, from the five loaves
of barley and the two fish; you who listened to Elisha and fed a thousand people with the ten barley loaves, listen to me today. You who listened to Daniel when he was in the lions’ den
and sent Habakkuk to him with the meal in his hands, listen to me today and send me bread from heaven, so that I may eat with my brothers and my fathers.” Immediately,
look, a table appeared with a dish on it, and three warm loaves on the dish. They ate in our midst [?]. My father said to them, “Get up, and let us eat the bread from heaven.”
He also took a little salt and put it on the table. We prayed together and ate the little bread with the Lord’s blessing. My father spoke and said to the brothers, “I tell you, it has been
fifty-four years since the day when my beloved father Apa Hyperichus shaved my head on the mountain. Until now, a single loaf has been allotted to me by God every forty [?]

days, along with a measure of water. I do not know where they come from. I eat some of them on the evening of my fortieth day, and I do not eat again until the completion of my next forty days, according to the commandment the Savior gave us

in the holy Gospel. He himself neither ate nor drank for forty days and forty nights.” The brothers said to him, “You are doing well. An athlete does not receive a crown unless he fights well.” He raised
his hands toward heaven and prayed with the brothers, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings, listen to us today and send us warm, fresh bread.” Immediately, look, [?]

from heaven. They ate in our midst [?], wrapped in fine linen cloths. Peter said to John, “Here are the bread and the cloths. We also need the equipment for the offering.” John answered and said to the brothers, “Pray for me, so that I may do what he [?].”
[?] John opened his mouth and said, “Our Lord Jesus Christ, send a table from heaven so that we may place your body on it.
and your blood.” Immediately, a golden table came from heaven and came to rest in our midst. Paul also rose and prayed in this way, saying, “My Lord
Jesus Christ, you who called me to a place among the holy apostles, although I was formerly a persecutor, persecuting his holy bride, the Church,
Now, Lord, listen to me in the midst of my brothers and send me from heaven a cup filled with wine from the true vine.” At that very moment, look, a cup filled
with wine from the true vine settled on the table. The old man Apa Isidore, the priest, also got up, raised both his hands toward heaven, and prayed, saying,
“Lord God Almighty, King of kings, I am not worthy to speak in the midst of my brothers and your chosen ones, whom you chose for yourself as apostles. But because of the joy you have given me,
I have risen and called upon you to grant my request and send me some perfume from the perfume of paradise, so that we may offer it while we invoke your name over your body
and your holy blood.” Immediately, look, a bowl filled with perfume settled in the midst. We were swimming in its fragrance. Apa Agathonicus, from the mountain of [?], also got up [?]. He said [?].
[?] pieces that were left [?] were put into my father’s basket. I drank the water in the jug. We prayed and left that place, and we went south through the whole mountain region [?].

[?] the brother monks. We heard a voice saying, “[?] bless us, Apa Paul of Tamma and Ezekiel, the youngest of them. Come in, holy ones of the Lord! Welcome to us, Apa Paul of Tamma, whom the Lord raised [?].”
[?] you here today.” My father said, “Greetings to you, Apa Pamun, wearer of many-colored clothing like that of Joseph, the righteous king
.” He asked him again, “Who shaved your head?” He said, “It was my father Apa Hellen. Remember me, my holy father, before [?].”
“My father, [?] where do you celebrate the liturgy on Saturday and Sunday?” Apa Pamun answered, “John the virgin is the one who celebrates the liturgy on Saturday and Sunday. For on Saturdays [?].”
As for Apa Apollo, we found him sitting on a throne, teaching his children the commandments of life. When he saw my father Apa Paul, he sprang up from his throne
He embraced him and kissed him, saying, “Welcome to us today, warrior of Christ, Apa Paul, whom the Lord raised from the dead five
times. He will raise you once more, just as he told you. And the seventh time he raises you will be on the day of the resurrection of all the saints.”

After Apa Apollo had said these things, he had all the people gathered together. He went to the church, and we celebrated the liturgy with the holy offering. He sent the brothers to the dining room, but he took us
to the service quarters and had food prepared for us to eat. My father, however, did not want to eat, because he had spent three days fasting during Lent. But our father Apa Apollo stood up

and urged him, saying, “Listen to me, my father, and eat with me, so that a blessing may come upon my dwelling and my community today because of you. You know, my beloved father, that it is not what enters
a person’s mouth that defiles the person. So now, my father, listen to me and eat with me.” My father agreed to eat with Apa Apollo. My companion and I also ate
together, with the rest of the brothers who were with us. Their names were Apa Paese, Apa Nishchroou, Apa Soures, and Apa Pita. When we had finished eating, in the evening, our father
Apa Apollo came among us and clapped his hands together, saying, “Let whoever has received wings fly away!” Immediately Apa Paese flew away and hurried to the mountain of Hache.
Apa Nishchroou also flew away and went to the mountain north of Antinoe. Apa Pitta also flew away and went to the mountain of Asyut. When this had happened, our father Apa Apollo led us out

to the south of the monastery as well. He embraced us and sent us away in peace. We traveled south through Mount Tereb until we reached Mount Terotashans, south of Qus. We found some antelopes down below,
down to a valley, where there was a monk among them. My father hurried forward and greeted him. He said to him, “What is your name?” He said, “My name is Aphou. Remember me, my father Apa Paul,

so that the Lord may bring me to a good end.” My father said to him, “How many years have you been in this place?” He said, “Fifty-four years.” My father asked him again, “Who put the monastic habit on you?” He said,

“It was Apa Anthony of Scetis.” My father said to him, “Then what do you live on as you roam with these antelopes?” He said, “My food and that of these antelopes is the same: the produce of the fields

and these wild herbs.” My father said to him, “Do you not freeze in winter or burn in summer?” He said to him, “When it is winter, I sleep among these antelopes, and they warm me with the breath from their mouths.
When it is summer, they gather together and stand over me, shading me so that the scorching heat does not trouble me.” My father said to him, “Truly, you deserve to be called Apa Aphou the Antelope.”
Immediately a voice came to us, saying, “This is his name throughout all the generations of the earth.”
We were amazed at what had happened so suddenly. We greeted him, departed from him, and traveled south to the mountain of Pshchepohe. We found a dwelling to the west of us.
My father knocked on the stone three times, according to the rule of the brother monks.
Immediately we heard a faint voice saying, “Bless me, my holy fathers.”
Then he came out and opened the door for us. We bowed down before him and greeted him.
His body had become very weak from hunger and thirst. He took us into his lodging. We prayed, sat down, and spoke about the great deeds of God.
My father said to him, “What is your name?”
He answered, saying, “My name is Phib, and I am from Perchous in the district of Touho.”
My father said to him, “How many years has it been since you came to this place?”
He said, “It has been eighteen years ...”
My father said to him, “How long will you remain in this place?”
He said to him again, “This is my dwelling in life and in death.”
My father said to him, “What do you eat, or what do you drink? Or who takes care of you?”
The holy Apa Phib answered, “Since the time of my youth, when I left my home, right up to today—
wherever I live, each time I complete my forty-day fast, I find a loaf of bread and a jug of water set before me.
and God is my witness—from that time on, one loaf has been allotted to me at a time.
But when you came to me today with your disciple, look, God sent us food for the three of us.”
Now get up, and let us taste a little bread, as God has commanded.”

We got up, stretched out our hands, and prayed. We stretched ourselves out and ate together from a single loaf. We also drank a little water. We left our father Apa Phoeb, and he sent us on our way in peace.
We traveled south through the whole mountain region until we reached the mountain of Meroeit, where we found ourselves a place to live.
I was sitting alone in the dwelling when a man came to the door and called to me.
I went outside to see what was happening.
He said to me, “Are you Ezekiel?”
I said to him, “Yes, I am.”
He said to me, “Let me inside the door of your dwelling so that I can tell you this matter.
“No, I do not want to tell it and have the brothers hear it and become afraid.”
Because of his pleasant way of speaking, I took him inside.
He said to me, “My brother Ezekiel, do you know what has happened?”
I said, “No.”

He said to me, “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, I was walking in the desert with some other men. We were looking for stones to make into smooth plaster. We encountered robbers in the mountains, and they took our equipment from us. We barely managed to escape from them alive.
After we escaped from their hands, we came upon a large man lying bound in a ravine.
We untied him.”
He said to us, ‘Leave me here. But when you go to the mountain, you will find this dwelling. Call inside, “Ezekiel!”’”
Your father said, “Come to me in the desert, for the robbers rose up and bound me, wanting to kill me. But God rescued my soul from their hands.”
We asked him, “What is your name?”
He said to us, “My name is Paul, and I am from Tamma in the district of Kois.”
When I, Ezekiel, heard these things, I was disturbed because he had mentioned my father’s name and his village.
That man said to me again, “Get up and follow me, and I will take you to him, for I see that you are afraid.”
I walked with him throughout the desert. I spent the first day and the second day walking.
I said to him, “Have we not yet reached that place?”
He said, “No. We had reached the third day of our journey through the desert.”
I said to him again, “Have we still not reached him?”
He said, “Look, we have come close to him.”
While he was speaking with me, he changed and became a huge Ethiopian, his eyes full of blood and his whole body covered with hair. He was [?], like bats.
He said to me, “Did you not recognize me, Ezekiel?
I said to him, “No.” He said to me, “I was the one making the spring run dry at that time. Your father struck me until I filled it again as it had been before.
I have worn myself out opposing you and your father, but you have not learned any sense.”
I said to him, “So you are the devil! May the Lord rebuke you for all the evil things you have done to Christ’s servants!”
He sprang at me like a wild lion, wanting to kill me.
But I cried out, “My father, help me!”
Immediately my father heard my voice as though he were close to me. He got up at once and came to me through God’s help.

When my father approached him, the devil immediately changed and took the form of a monk, wearing an animal skin and small palm-leaf sandals. He approached my father and bowed down at his feet according to the rule of the monastic brothers.
Immediately my father struck him around his monastic habit [?], because he realized that he was the devil.
He seized him, bound him hand and foot, and rolled him down into a ravine. We left him there and went on our way.
I said to my father, “What is this thing you have done to this shameless creature?”
My father said to me, “God handed him over to me so that I could punish him as I wished, because he dared to tempt us.”
After my father said these things, we got up and returned to our dwelling, giving glory to God.

My father spent forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking, sitting on a brick inside the dwelling and staring at a window through an opening. He did not close his eyes during these forty days, until they burst and fell out onto the ground.
The holy archangel came from heaven—that is, Michael the archangel—at dawn on Sunday, at the completion of the forty days.
He made the sign of the cross over him and brought all his sufferings to an end. His eyes became steady as before. Michael the archangel went up to heaven in glory.
We gathered with the brothers who were with us in that place and ate with them on the Lord’s Day. Then we left them in peace.
We went south to the rock of Asyut and found ourselves a small place to live there.
My father practiced great acts of ascetic discipline.
One day a great saint of God came to us. His name was Apa Bishoy of Jeremiah, and he lived on the mountain of Qaw, east of the river.
We greeted one another, prayed, and sat down. We spoke about the greatness of Christ and the ways of life of the saints.
When they had finished discussing with one another, we got up and walked on the mountain. We found a rock full of corpses. They had all been idol worshipers.
When the saints reached them, they stood and prayed over them. They all rose alive, numbering six hundred men and fifty-four women.
The saints said to them, “What is your occupation?”
One of them spoke up and said, “Listen to me, holy ones, and I will tell you about our wickedness and our lawlessness.
For we are a single nation, worshiping a wild animal called the wolf. We care for it at all times, offering it little children three years old as sacrifices.
He used to encourage us, saying, ‘Do deeds like these,’ and other deeds worse than these, which we do not wish to mention.
Now, then, my holy fathers, let your mercy reach us, and baptize us as Christians are baptized, for the suffering that lies upon us is great.”
Christ’s farmer, Apa Bishoy of Jeremiah, answered, “Get up, and let us pray to God that he may give us assurance about this matter.”
My father said, “Let us pray.”
They rose and called upon God together, saying, “God, merciful and compassionate, who sent his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who died for the beings he had formed,

and set the world free through the blessing of holy baptism, have compassion on these servants of yours who stand here today, awaiting your mercy and compassion, so that they may receive forgiveness [?]
